2. The pre-emptor-opposite-party Nos.1-5 filed Miscellaneous (Pre-emption) Case No.31 of 2005 against the pre emptee-petitioner and others in the Court of Assistant Judge, Rajbari Sadar, Rajbari for pre-emption of the case property measuring an area of 34 decimals out of SA plot No. 339, now plot No. 240 appertaining to S A Khatian No. 367 (DP Khatian No, 560) of Mouza Bilnoyabad under Police Station and District-Rajbari. Their case, in short, is that one Komala Krishna Guha was the owner-in-possession of plot No.240 and on his death, it devolved upon his daughter Boiashakhi alias Owisharjya Guha. The pre-emptor-opposite-party No.1 along with others was the owner-in-possession of plot No. 338 appertaining to SA Khatian No. 239 of the self-same Mouza Bilnoyabad. Anyway, one Shanti Rani Guha was the owner-in-possession of previous plot No. 362 at Bilnoyabad Mouza. At one stage, Shanti Rani Guha transferred the plot No. 362 to one Md Hekmat Ali Munshi by a registered deed dated 2-12-1986. After the death of Md Hekmat Ali Munshi, his heirs transferred the said plot No. 362 in favour of the pre-emptor-- opposite-party Nos. 2-5 by a registered deed dated 7-5-1997. The previous plot No. 362 was converted into plot No. 241 and accordingly the relevant Khatian was published. The previous plot No. 338 of the pre-emptor-opposite-party No.1 was converted into plot No. 238 and he has been in possession thereof for about 50 (fifty) years. In this way, the pre-emptor-opposite-party Nos.1-5 have been the contiguous landholders of the case plot No. 240. However, the pre-emptee-petitioner purchased the case property from Boishakhi by a registered kabala dated 9-5-2004. The pre-emptor-opposite-party Nos. 1-5 came to know about the Kabala dated 9-5-2004 on 11-12-2004 for the first time and thereafter they obtained the certified copy of the said kabala on 11-5-2005. They are entitled to get the case property by way of pre-emption as contiguous landholders under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Act, 1950. 

 11. Mr Zakir Hossain Bhuiyan also submits that the right of pre-emption is a statutory right under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 and this statutory right of pre-emption cannot be defeated by mere verbal assurance of the person having such right, unless other facts and circumstances clearly make out a case of acquiescence or waiver. In this connection, he has drawn my attention to the decision in the case of Fazaruddin vs Maijuddin reported in 44 DLR (AD) 62.
